title: Personal Hygiene, Sanitation and Continuous Cleaning

lessons.title: Personal hygiene in the abattoir
lessons.html:
People can contaminate meat

Every worker in an abattoir, including the meat examiner, can carry bacteria on hands, hair, skin, nose and clothes. Good personal hygiene protects consumers, the abattoir's licence under the Meat Safety Act 40 of 2000, and the workers themselves.

Health of workers

  • Workers must be medically fit to handle meat. Abattoirs keep health records as required.
  • Report illness immediately: diarrhoea, vomiting, fever, skin infections, boils or a discharging ear, eye or nose. You may need to stay away from meat handling until cleared.
  • Cover cuts and wounds with waterproof, brightly coloured dressings, and wear gloves over them.

Protective clothing

  • Clean overalls or coats, changed at least daily or when dirty.
  • Hair covering (cap or hair net) and beard covers where needed.
  • White or light-coloured clothing so dirt is easy to see.
  • Waterproof aprons, boots and, where required, cut-resistant gloves and arm guards.
  • Different colour clothing for clean and dirty areas helps stop people moving between zones without changing.
  • Protective clothing is never worn outside the plant, to the toilet or canteen.

Hand washing

Wash hands at the start of work, after breaks, after the toilet, after touching the hide, gut, floor, face or hair, after handling waste, and whenever they become dirty. Use warm water and liquid soap, rub all surfaces of hands, wrists and between fingers, rinse and dry with disposable paper towels. Hand-wash basins should be non-hand operated (knee or foot taps).

Behaviour

  • No eating, drinking, smoking, chewing gum or spitting in production areas.
  • No jewellery, watches, false nails or nail polish.
  • Keep nails short and clean.
  • Do not cough or sneeze over meat.
  • Use footbaths and boot washers when entering production areas.

lessons.title: Sanitation and continuous cleaning
lessons.html:
Keeping the plant clean

Cleaning versus disinfecting

Cleaning removes visible dirt, fat, blood and meat particles. Disinfecting (sanitising) kills most remaining micro-organisms. Disinfectants do not work properly on dirty surfaces, so cleaning always comes first.

Standard cleaning steps

  1. Dry clean: remove meat scraps, fat and waste by hand or scraper.
  2. Pre-rinse with water to remove loose soil.
  3. Apply detergent (usually foam) and allow the contact time on the label.
  4. Scrub where needed.
  5. Rinse off detergent with clean water.
  6. Disinfect with an approved sanitiser at the correct concentration and contact time.
  7. Final rinse if the product label requires it, then allow to drain and dry.

Work from top to bottom and from clean areas towards dirty areas and drains, so you do not splash dirt onto cleaned surfaces.

Continuous cleaning during production

Cleaning is not only at the end of the shift. During slaughter:

  • Sterilise knives and steels in hot water sterilisers between carcasses and whenever contaminated, at the temperature the regulations require.
  • Clean hand tools, saws and aprons regularly using the hot water and wash stations on the line.
  • Remove waste and condemned material continuously into marked containers.
  • Squeegee floors and keep drains clear to prevent splashing.
  • Do not hose down floors near exposed meat during production, as spray carries bacteria onto carcasses.

Chemical safety

Detergents and sanitisers can burn skin and eyes. Wear gloves, goggles and aprons, never mix chemicals (especially chlorine products with acids), store them in a locked area away from meat, and keep safety data sheets available. Chemicals must be approved for use in food plants.

Checking cleaning

Supervisors and meat examiners inspect before production starts. Swab tests sent to a laboratory or rapid tests verify that surfaces are truly clean. Record results and corrective actions.

Key points

  • Report illness and cover wounds before handling meat.
  • Wear clean protective clothing and never wear it outside the plant.
  • Wash hands often, with soap and non-hand-operated taps.
  • Clean first, then disinfect; work top to bottom and clean to dirty.
  • Clean continuously during production and verify cleaning with inspections and swabs.

quiz.question: What must a worker with diarrhoea do?

options.text: Work as normal but wash hands more
Report it to the supervisor immediately

quiz.question: Why do disinfectants come after cleaning?

options.text: They do not work properly on dirty surfaces

quiz.question: In which direction should cleaning be done?

options.text: Top to bottom and clean towards dirty

quiz.question: Why are hand-wash basins knee- or foot-operated?

options.text: So clean hands do not touch dirty taps
